Maladaptive Strategies.value: go over and over why the event happened to me
I work hard at keeping busy with other things
repeatedly blame myself for what happened

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt

vignette: Maria, a 78-year-old Latin American woman and librarian, has been struggling with symptoms that have progressively worsened since her traumatic experience as a refugee. Now married to her long-time partner of many years, she recounts the harrowing events that occurred decades ago in vivid detail, but finds it nearly impossible to put those memories into words. The event Maria describes is deeply entrenched in her mind and often triggered by specific sensory cues. For instance, when she smells certain scents reminiscent of the camp where she was held captive, such as the acrid smell of smoke from burning trash or the pungent odor of unwashed bodies, intense feelings of guilt and fear are rekindled. This olfactory recall triggers a sharp rise in her hypervigilance, making her feel superalert and on guard, especially when she is outside the few places she considers safe. Maria’s hypervigilant state only exacerbates her rumination and self-blame. She constantly goes over why the event happened to her, believing that if she had made different choices or acted differently, things might have turned out better. This relentless cycle of self-criticism and guilt is a constant in her life, deeply affecting her ability to concentrate on tasks at work and home. Her intense hypervigilance also leads her to only feel safe within the confines of her home, further isolating her from the community she once thrived in as a librarian. The safety she finds here provides temporary relief but does not alleviate the underlying trauma. Instead, it reinforces the belief that the world outside is fraught with danger, which in turn fuels her hypervigilance and self-blame. As Maria has grown older, her job as a librarian has become both a refuge and a source of anxiety. The quietness of the library offers some respite from intrusive memories, but the daily tasks remind her of the trauma she seeks to forget. She often finds herself engrossed in work to keep her mind occupied, trying to avoid the painful thoughts that lurk just beneath the surface. Maria’s self-blame and rumination have created a vicious cycle where her maladaptive strategies further intensify her memories and hypervigilance. Each time she remembers an event, the associated guilt is overwhelming, making it even more difficult for her to function normally outside of her safe space. This has led her to withdraw from social activities and gatherings, which once were a significant part of her life. Her husband notices the changes in Maria’s behavior but feels at a loss on how to help. She often expresses that what frightens her most is losing herself entirely to these intrusive thoughts and memories. Despite her efforts to keep busy and avoid triggers, she knows that something needs to change. Maria finally decided to seek help when she realized that her withdrawal was affecting her relationship with her husband and her ability to enjoy simple pleasures like reading or spending time outside. She hopes for a way to manage the overwhelming guilt and hypervigilance so she can live without constantly feeling trapped in the past, and instead find peace and comfort in the present. Her current state is marked by an intense fear of losing control over her thoughts and memories, which has left her feeling isolated and desperate. Maria’s goal is clear: to regain a sense of safety and normalcy that allows her to live without being overwhelmed by the echoes of her traumatic past.
